faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.q1: Do I need a visa (Japan / Korea)?
faq.a1:
Japan: Citizens of the Czech Republic and Slovakia can enter visa-free for tourist stays up to 90 days. A valid passport is sufficient.

South Korea: Currently, Czech and Slovak citizens are exempt from K-ETA registration (until the end of 2024), so a valid passport is also enough. However, the situation may change, and we will always inform you in time.
faq.q2: How large will my group be?
faq.a2: Our tours are designed for small groups, usually 8 to 12 people. Exceptions can be made — for example, if 3 couples and one large family travel together, they'll naturally be in one group. We also welcome solo travelers, though there may be a slightly higher price if you require your own room.
faq.q3: How physically demanding is the program?
faq.a3: Our tours have a difficulty level of about 2/5. However, expect to walk at least 15 kilometers per day. We frequently use public transport (trains, metro), so stairs and walking transfers are unavoidable.
faq.q4: Can I pay by card everywhere, or do I need cash (yen)?
faq.a4: Japan has made tremendous progress toward cashless payments, but you still need local cash. You'll encounter countless street food alleys, small shops near shrines, and ticket machines where cash is the only option. We recommend always having at least 10,000 JPY in your wallet.
faq.a5: In Japan, tipping is not customary. It's considered part of the price, and attempting to tip may embarrass the staff or be seen as rude. Quality service is the standard here and doesn't require extra payment.
faq.q6: Can I smoke in public in Japan?
faq.a6: Street smoking is prohibited in most major cities (except designated 'Smoking Areas'). Walking while smoking can result in a fine. However, there are indoor smoking rooms in buildings, some restaurants, and at train stations.
faq.q7: How much do basic items cost at 7-Eleven (konbini)?
faq.a7:
Konbini stores (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are great sources of affordable, quality food 24/7. Approximate prices:
• Onigiri (rice ball): 150 JPY
• Sandwich / Sweet pastry: 250–350 JPY
• Hot Bento (main meal): 500–750 JPY
• Coffee / Beverages: 100–200 JPY
faq.q8: Where can I find trash cans in Japan?
faq.a8: Public trash cans on the street are almost nonexistent. Japanese people carry their trash home. Bins are usually found near vending machines (for bottles and cans only) or at konbini entrances (where you're expected to discard items purchased there).
faq.q9: Do I need a power adapter?
faq.a9: Yes, Japan uses Type A/B plugs (two flat pins, same as the US). The voltage is 100V. Most modern chargers (phones, laptops) work in the 100–240V range, but for a European hair dryer or kettle, you'd need a transformer (which isn't worth it).
faq.q10: Can I visit an onsen (hot spring) with tattoos?
faq.a10: Traditionally, tattoos are banned in onsens due to their historical association with the Yakuza. Some baths allow tattooed visitors if the tattoo is small enough to cover with a bandage. Increasingly, 'tattoo-friendly' onsens are appearing, and we'll be happy to recommend some.
faq.askDesc: Didn't find your answer? Write us directly — we'll respond within 24 hours.
faq.askPlaceholderQuestion: What would you like to ask?

Osaka.desc: The culinary capital of Japan with a friendly atmosphere and a famous castle.

Hiroshima.desc: A city of peace with a poignant history, near which lies the sacred island of Miyajima.

Kanazawa.desc: A picturesque city with well-preserved samurai districts and one of the most beautiful gardens.

Kagoshima.desc: The Naples of the East, located on a bay with the active volcano Sakurajima.

Nagasaki.desc: A port city with rich European and Chinese cultural influences and a complex history.

Kumamoto.desc: A city known for one of the largest and most beautiful castles in Japan.

Okinawa (Naha).desc: A tropical paradise with stunning beaches, unique Ryukyu culture, and delicious food.

Kamakura.desc: A coastal town full of Zen temples and the famous statue of the Great Buddha.

Yokohama.desc: The second largest city with modern architecture and a huge Chinatown.

Sapporo.desc: The capital of Hokkaido island, famous for beer, ramen, and the snow festival.

Soul (Seoul).desc: The vibrant capital of South Korea, where modern skyscrapers stand next to ancient palaces.

cancel.title: Cancellation Terms | Ted's Eastern World
cancel.heading: Cancellation Terms
cancel.lastUpdated: Effective from January 1, 2026 | Last update: May 2026
cancel.bindingText: The reservation becomes binding after paying a deposit of 30% of the total tour price. Until the deposit is paid, we reserve the right to offer the spot to another applicant.
cancel.feesDesc: The cancellation fee depends on the number of days before departure when you notify us:
cancel.insuranceText: Cancellation fees are not covered by standard health insurance. We recommend getting travel insurance with cancellation coverage — we're happy to help you choose.
cancel.step1Title: Contact us via email or phone
cancel.step1Text: Write to us at sykoratadeas2001@gmail.com or use the contact page. Include your name, date, and reservation number.
cancel.step2Text: Within 48 hours, you'll receive an email confirming the cancellation and any applicable fees.
cancel.step3Text: We will process the refund within 14 business days from the cancellation confirmation to the account from which the payment was made.
cancel.healthText: In the case of serious illness (documented by a medical report) or unforeseen force majeure events (natural disaster, pandemic), we handle each case individually and are always willing to find a fair solution.
cancel.rescheduleText: Instead of cancellation, the reservation can be transferred to another available date free of charge — no later than 30 days before departure (one-time only).
cancel.ctaQuestion: Have a question about cancellation or need help?

section.historySamuraiDesc: For centuries, the country was ruled by military commanders (shoguns) and samurai. The Edo period (1603-1867) brought peace and isolation.
section.historyMeijiDesc: In 1868, power was restored to the emperor. Japan opened to the world and quickly modernized into an industrial power.
section.historyModernDesc: Today, Japan is a leader in technology, pop culture (anime/manga), while maintaining deep traditions.
section.figOdaDesc: A ruthless warlord who initiated the unification of Japan in the 16th century.
section.figTokugawaDesc: The founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for over 250 years in relative peace.
section.figHokusaiDesc: One of the most famous Japanese artists and creator of the famous woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa.
section.cityTokyoDesc: A fascinating metropolis where neon skyscrapers stand just steps from peaceful Shinto shrines. It's a culinary paradise with the most Michelin stars in the world and a city that never sleeps.
section.cityKyotoDesc: The heart of traditional Japan with over 2000 Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines. Stroll through the preserved Gion and Higashiyama districts, where you might spot a real geisha.
section.cityOsakaDesc: A city with a relaxed atmosphere, friendly people, and unbeatable street food. The city's motto is kuidaore (eat until you drop), best experienced in the bustling Dotonbori district.

dest.heroDesc: Destination guide — culture, history, cuisine, and everything you need to know for an unforgettable trip to the Land of the Rising Sun.
dest.title: Japan
dest.intro1: Japan (Japanese: 日本, Nihon or Nippon) is an island country in the northwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of four main islands — Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku — and over 6,800 smaller islands. With a history spanning over 2,000 years, Japan is home to a unique civilization that harmoniously blends ancient traditions with cutting-edge technology.
dest.intro2: Japan is the world's third-largest economy and a cultural superpower whose influence — from anime and manga to sushi, karate, design, and robotics — is truly global. The Land of the Rising Sun attracts over 30 million tourists annually.
dest.gal3: Fushimi Inari — thousands of torii gates
dest.gal4: Kyoto — city of temples and geishas
dest.hist1Desc: Japan was unified under an imperial dynasty around 700 AD. Culture was strongly influenced by China — kanji script, Buddhism, and Confucianism were adopted.
dest.hist2Desc: Samurai and shoguns ruled Japan for centuries. The Edo period (1603–1867) brought 250 years of peace, prosperity, and cultural flourishing under near-total isolation from the world.
dest.hist3Desc: Japan opened up to the world and within a single generation transformed from a medieval feudal society into a modern industrial power comparable to Europe.
dest.hist4Desc: After WWII, Japan became a democratic country and an economic miracle. Today, it's a global leader in technology, robotics, and pop culture.
dest.cult1Desc: The cherry blossom (sakura) viewing festival is one of the most important Japanese traditions. In late March and early April, Japanese gather in parks.
dest.cult2Desc: Japan has thousands of local festivals with parades, fireworks, and traditional dances. The most famous are Gion Matsuri in Kyoto and Awa Odori in Tokushima.
dest.cult3Desc: Japan is the birthplace of karate, judo, aikido, kendo, and sumo. Sumo is the national sport with a tradition stretching back over 1,500 years.
dest.cult4Desc: Japanese animated culture has conquered the world. Studio Ghibli (Hayao Miyazaki) and franchises like Dragon Ball, One Piece, or Naruto have billions of fans globally.
dest.cuisineDesc: Japanese cuisine (washoku) is inscribed on the UNESCO list. It's renowned for the freshness of ingredients, elegance of presentation, and variety of flavors. Tokyo has more Michelin stars than any other city.
dest.fig1Desc: A ruthless warlord who initiated the unification of Japan. His tactics and modernization of the army changed Japanese military history forever.
dest.fig2Desc: Founder of the Edo shogunate that ruled Japan for 250 years. Under his leadership, the longest era of peace in Japanese history occurred.
dest.fig3Desc: Creator of the iconic woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa, which influenced European Impressionism. One of the first globally recognized Japanese artists.
dest.fig4Desc: Founder of Studio Ghibli and an animation genius. Films like My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away are global cinematic treasures.
dest.r1Sub: Reigning since May 2019 — Reiwa era (令和 — 'Beautiful Harmony')
dest.r2Sub: In office since February 2025 — Liberal Democratic Party (LDP)

section.historyThreeKingdomsDesc: From the 1st century BC to the 7th century AD, the Korean peninsula was ruled by the Three Kingdoms: Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla.
section.historyJoseonDesc: The longest-ruling dynasty (1392–1897), which created the Korean alphabet Hangul and deeply rooted Confucianism into society.
section.historyModernDesc: After WWII and the Korean War (1950–1953), the peninsula split. South Korea transformed from a poor nation into a technological and cultural (K-pop) superpower.
section.figSejongDesc: The fourth ruler of the Joseon Dynasty, who created and promulgated the brilliant Korean alphabet Hangul in the 15th century.
section.figYiSunShinDesc: A brilliant naval commander who repelled Japanese invasions in the 16th century using the legendary "turtle ships".
section.figBongJoonHoDesc: A world-renowned director who made cinematic history with Parasite, the first foreign-language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture.
section.citySeoulDesc: A vibrant capital where modern skyscrapers and innovative technology blend with ancient palaces like Gyeongbokgung. A paradise for shopping and street food.
section.cityBusanDesc: The second largest city and main port. Offers beautiful beaches like Haeundae, the colorful Gamcheon Culture Village, and the freshest seafood at Jagalchi Market.
section.cityJejuDesc: A volcanic island in the south, known as the "Hawaii of Korea". Famous for its lava tubes, beautiful waterfalls, beaches, and the unique Haenyeo diver culture.

dest.heroDesc: Destination guide — dynamic culture, turbulent history, spicy cuisine, and everything for a perfect trip to the heart of Asia.
dest.title: South Korea
dest.intro1: South Korea (Korean: 대한민국, Daehan Minguk) is a country occupying the southern half of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia. With a population of over 51 million, half of whom live in the Seoul metropolitan area, it is one of the most densely populated countries in the world. Following the devastating Korean War, the country underwent phenomenal economic growth, known as the Miracle on the Han River.
dest.intro2: Today, South Korea is a global leader in information technology, electronics (Samsung, LG), and the automotive industry (Hyundai, Kia). K-Pop (BTS, Blackpink), K-Dramas, and Korean cosmetics have taken the world by storm through a phenomenon known as "Hallyu" (the Korean Wave).
dest.hist1Desc: A dynasty that ruled Korea for over 500 years (1392-1897). During this time, the Korean alphabet Hangul was created, and Confucianism became the state ideology.
dest.hist2Desc: The Korean peninsula was annexed by Japan. This difficult period only ended with Japan's surrender at the end of World War II.
dest.hist3Desc: A conflict that permanently divided the peninsula into the communist North and capitalist South. It ended only with an armistice; technically, the war never ended.
dest.hist4Desc: Within a few decades, devastated South Korea became one of the world's strongest economies thanks to massive industrialization and education.
dest.cult1Desc: Traditional Korean clothing with vibrant colors and simple lines. Today, it is mainly worn during holidays or visits to historical palaces.
dest.cult2Desc: Korean popular music and dramas (K-Dramas) have become a global phenomenon, spreading Korean culture all over the world.
dest.cult3Desc: A philosophy deeply rooted in Korean society, emphasizing respect for elders, education, and family hierarchy.
dest.cult4Desc: South Korea is considered the birthplace of professional video gaming. E-sports is a national sport here with millions of viewers.
dest.cuisineDesc: Korean cuisine is renowned for its spiciness, fermented side dishes, and shared meals. Tabletop meat grilling and countless side dishes (banchan) are typical. Kimchi — fermented cabbage — is the national dish and is UNESCO listed.
dest.fig1Desc: The most revered monarch in Korean history. He championed the creation of the Korean alphabet Hangul to enable education even for commoners.
dest.fig2Desc: A national hero who repelled the Japanese invasion using innovative armored "turtle ships". He never lost a single battle.
dest.fig3Desc: A famous Korean film director. His film Parasite became the first non-English language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture.
dest.fig4Desc: The most famous K-Pop group in the world. They were the first Korean artists to conquer the US Billboard charts and became global cultural ambassadors.
dest.r1Sub: In office since May 2027 — Democratic Party of Korea
dest.r2Sub: Modern headquarters in Seoul that replaced the traditional Blue House (Cheong Wa Dae).
